title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
hook: the twins fall next, the wise one and the beautiful one, and the reason given is the same small sentence twice
carry: no one is equal to me
tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday on the Pandavas' last journey, Draupadi fell first in the sea of sand, and Bhima was the one who stopped to ask why. Your line was she loved Arjuna more than the rest of us. Did you stop for someone who fell behind? Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Sahadeva and Nakula are the youngest of the five, the twins, sons of Madri, raised by Kunti as her own. In this serial they have often stood just behind their older brothers. Sahadeva, known for his learning. Nakula, known as the handsome one. Now, on the road toward Meru, Sahadeva falls. A little later, Nakula falls too. Both times, Bhima calls out to the front of the line, and both times Yudhishthira answers without stopping. Today, the twins, and what he says about them.
screen: `THE TWINS, SONS OF MADRI.` → `SAHADEVA FALLS.` → `THEN NAKULA.`

segments.voice: Listen to the shape of Yudhishthira's answers. About Sahadeva, in Ganguli's telling: he thought no one was equal to him in wisdom. About Nakula: he thought no one was equal to him in beauty. That's it. The same sentence, twice, with one word changed. Look at what isn't blamed. Not the learning. Not the good looks. Those are gifts, and the epic has praised both brothers for them. What trips each of them is a small private thought laid on top of the gift: no one is equal to me. Sahadeva's wisdom could have walked on with him. What he couldn't carry to the top of the world, in this telling, was the comparison. The same goes for Nakula's face. Notice, too, who asks. Bhima, the strongest of them, is the one calling out each time, and Yudhishthira answers only what he is asked. The pride he names here is not a boast spoken aloud. It's a quiet habit of measuring, held inside. And on a road this steep, every extra ounce counts. Behind the line, the dog still walks. Three travelers are left with Yudhishthira now: Bhima, Arjuna and the dog. The road narrows as the people on it fall away, and the question Bhima keeps asking, why, gets the same kind of answer every time.
screen: `"NONE EQUAL TO HIM IN WISDOM"` · `"NONE EQUAL TO HIM IN BEAUTY"` · `NOT THE GIFT, THE COMPARISON` · then, large: `PRIDE AS A HABIT OF MEASURING`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you're genuinely good at. Don't be modest. Breathe in and simply be glad of it. Breathe out and notice whether a second thought comes attached, a comparison, a ranking, someone you're better than. If it does, don't argue with it. Just set that second thought down and keep the gift. Breathe that way for a while: the gift in, the comparison out. If you pray, you can give thanks for the gift. The bell holds the time.
Sahadeva. The youngest Pandava, known for his wisdom, who falls on the road for thinking no one his equal in it.
Your line: no one is equal to me. Today, when you catch yourself measuring against someone, keep the gift and drop the comparison. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: The falls of Sahadeva and Nakula are told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva, and Hindu teachers sometimes use the sequence of falls to talk about the small faults that weigh down even good people.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Bhima asks why your learned youngest brother has fallen. what reason do you give?
options: he wasn't strong enough for the road.
he thought no one equal to him in wisdom.
fork.reveal: Yudhishthira says Sahadeva thought no one his equal in wisdom, and gives the same answer for Nakula and beauty.

original.note: Sahadeva: the youngest Pandava, known for his learning, who falls second.

trapdoor: what you thought: the twins are punished for being proud of their gifts.
what it means: the fault named is the comparison: thinking no one their equal.
what a scholar hears: Yudhishthira gives both twins one formula, none his equal, with only the gift changed.

notes: All paraphrase. The screen heads in quotation marks gloss Yudhishthira's answers; confirm the sense against Ganguli (Sahadeva: none his equal in wisdom; Nakula: none his equal in beauty).
Confirm that the twins fall in this order (Sahadeva, then Nakula) after Draupadi.
Sahadeva's learning and Nakula's beauty are drawn from the epic's own characterization; confirm.
The word "ounce" is a figure of speech, not a claim.
